title: 'They're not alone': Sister of Adam Sprague outraged by recent Orangeville jail cell overdose
article: The sister of a man who died inside an Orangeville Police Service jail cell nine years ago began "crying uncontrollably" upon learning a woman remains on life support in hospital after suffering a drug overdose while in police custody.

"I was under the impression that more training was to be given to the police force after what happened to my brother," said Lindsey Callaghan, the sister of Adam Sprague, who died due to a drug overdose in an OPS cell on Nov. 11, 2010.
"This proves it either didn't occur or the police just don't care," she said. "Something needs to be done about this."

Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) is probing the circumstances surrounding what happened to a woman who was arrested and put in a OPS cell before suffering a drug overdose while in police custody, during the early morning hours of June 2.
Initially, based on information provided by OPS, the SIU decided not to investigate.

After receiving additional information from a relative of the overdose victim on June 10, the police watchdog reversed that decision and invoked its mandate. As of June 17, the relative said the woman remained on life support in hospital.

Given the SIU's decision to launch a formal probe after being contacted by the relative, the question as to whether OPS was forthright with details it first provided the police watchdog needs answering.

"Based on the information and evidence shared with the SIU at the time, the SIU did not have grounds to invoke its mandate," SIU spokesperson Monica Hudon told the Banner, confirming OPS notified the SIU sometime after the woman was taken to hospital on June 2.
"The SIU operates based on the information at its disposal," she said. "It'd be premature to comment on the nature and extent of the information the SIU was initially provided."
The SIU has assigned one investigator to the case and has yet to identify any subject officers. Hudon said the SIU "did not attend" the OPS station prior to its initial decision not to investigate.

"We were just notified that the SIU has decided to review this matter and has now invoked their mandate," OPS Const. Scott Davis told the Banner at 3:50 p.m. on June10. "As such, I'm unable to provide you with a response to your questions at this time."
The Banner has spoken to the woman's relative who questioned the SIU's initial decision. She is concerned about police involvement while her relative was in custody.

The relative, who has not been named, to protect the identity of the overdose victim, alleges doctors have said the woman consumed "a large amount of drugs" inside the cell and suffered a seizure for at least 30 minutes.
"Every day, we see a little bit more (progress). But I feel that she won't be the same. She is going to need, I don't know, full-time care," the relative told the Banner last week.

"I'm not saying she isn't at fault. She is the one that took the drugs," she said. "But when the police take someone in their custody, I think they're liable to the point where they shouldn't allow that person to do drugs in their custody or should be supervising them."
Callaghan contacted the Banner after reading online about the recent incident at OPS. As she started "crying uncontrollably," she wished to relay a message on to the overdose victim's family.
"Please tell the family involved this time they're not alone," Callaghan told the Banner. "There are people that 100 per cent understand what they're going through. My heart goes out to them."
Sprague, who was wrongfully arrested for public intoxication, died of an oxycodone overdose while in a holding cell at the C Line police station early in the morning of Nov. 11, 2010.

Following a coroner's inquest, in May 2014 a five-person jury ruled Sprague's death was accidental. Along with that verdict, the jury made 33 recommendations for OPS, the local police board and several provincial agencies.
Among them were that OPS physically check on prisoners every 15 minutes. If a prisoner is sleeping, the jury recommended police rouse the person at least every 30 minutes.
After a probe into Sprague's death, the SIU announced that no criminal charges would be laid.
A lawsuit launched by Sprague's family against OPS was settled out of court. Further details about the terms of that settlement are not known.

Const. Jon Kennedy - not the subject officer of the SIU probe - subsequently pleaded guilty to discreditable conduct during a Police Service Act (PSA) hearing, after admitting he made an unlawful arrest.

Sgt. Chris Dryden, whom the SIU criticized but did not charge criminally for failing to physically check on Sprague in the jail cell overnight, pleaded guilty to two counts of discreditable conduct during a separate PSA hearing in June 2012.

At about 11 p.m. on June 1, Hudon said, police officers went to a residence on Church Street for what she described as a medical-related call. Upon their arrival, Hudon said, police investigated and arrested the woman before transporting her to the police station.

The woman's relative claimed that another person who had consumed drugs at the residence was taken to hospital. Davis has previously said the woman was arrested on a warrant for failing to attend court.

After the woman was booked and put in a holding cell, Hudon said, she was transported to hospital at about 2:30 a.m. on June 2. Her relative is in the process of attempting to obtain police reports and possibly video footage from the holding cell.
"There are a lot of unanswered questions," the relative said. "I'm not saying they are 100 per cent liable, but I feel they could have handled and made better choices."
